## Cards

### 01 · Pregnancy with type 1 or type 2
Group: **Seasons of life** · Referral chip: **Ask your pregnancy care team** · Products shown: *none*

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

**Before you try** `1.s1`

- Diabetes Canada’s guideline recommends planning a pregnancy with your diabetes team before you start trying `1.s1.1`
- Its A1C target before conception is 7.0% or lower, and 6.5% or lower if it can be done safely. Your team sets yours `1.s1.2`
- It recommends starting folic acid before you conceive. With diabetes, you may need a higher dose than is usually advised, so ask your team or pharmacist how much to take `1.s1.3`
- Bring a list of all your medicines, so your team can review them before you try. Some medicines need to be stopped or changed before pregnancy. Don’t stop any on your own `1.s1.4`
- The guideline recommends an eye exam and a kidney check before you conceive `1.s1.5`

**While you’re pregnant** `1.s2`

- Blood sugar targets are tighter in pregnancy. Your team will give you yours `1.s2.1`
- With type 1, Diabetes Canada’s guideline recommends a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) in pregnancy. With type 2, ask your team whether one suits you `1.s2.2`
- The guideline recommends another eye exam in the first trimester `1.s2.3`
- In pregnancy, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) can happen even when blood sugar is normal or only a little high. DKA needs medical care right away `1.s2.4`

**After the birth** `1.s3`

- If you use insulin, your needs drop quickly after the birth. Plan the change with your team before you deliver. Lows are more likely in the first days, so check more often `1.s3.1`
- The guideline encourages breastfeeding `1.s3.2`
- It also recommends an eye exam within the first year after the birth `1.s3.3`

> **Note** `1.note` — Gestational diabetes, which starts in pregnancy, is in Know Your Type. This card draws mostly on Diabetes Canada’s pregnancy guideline for health professionals and its key messages for people planning a pregnancy. That guideline is from 2018, and Diabetes Canada is updating it.

*Sources for this card:* Diabetes and Pregnancy (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Blood Glucose Monitoring in Adults and Children with Diabetes: Update 2021 (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Diabetic Retinopathy | See The Possibilities (Canadian Ophthalmological Society); Hyperglycemic Emergencies in Adults (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and ketones (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Gestational Diabetes (Diabetes Canada); Folic acid, healthy pregnancy and neural tube defect prevention (Public Health Agency of Canada)

### 02 · A child with type 1
Group: **Seasons of life** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `childGear` — mylife YpsoPump Kids Pouch (4323), Jerry the Bear (5017), Buzzy Personal LadyBuzz (4459)

- Diabetes Canada’s 2025 type 1 guideline sets the same A1C target for children of every age: below 7.0%. Your child’s team sets theirs `2.1`
- Younger children take less fast-acting sugar for a low, depending on their age. The amounts are in The Rule of 15 `2.2`
- From age 4, glucagon can be a nasal spray or an injection. For a child under 4, ask your child’s team which glucagon to keep `2.3`
- Check for ketones when your child is sick or their blood sugar stays high. The ranges are in Ketones: check and act `2.4`
- The guideline says regular check-ins on emotional health are especially helpful in the teen years and young adulthood `2.5`
- Type 1 diabetes meets the Disability Tax Credit’s life-sustaining therapy test for 2021 and later tax years. You still apply with form T2201, on paper or online, and your child’s doctor or nurse practitioner fills in their part `2.6`
- Once a child is approved for the credit, a Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP) can be opened for them `2.7`
- Some provincial pump programs have separate rules for children. In Quebec, a child has to join the pump program before age 18 `2.8`
- Kidney checks usually start 5 years after diagnosis, or after puberty if your child was diagnosed young. Eye exams usually start at age 15, once your child has had type 1 for 5 years. Your child’s team sets the schedule `2.9`

> **Note** `2.note` — Your child’s diabetes clinic is the first call for anything about their plan. Programs by province are in Funding & Coverage.

*Sources for this card:* Glycemic Management Across the Lifespan for People With Type 1 Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and ketones (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Mental Health and Diabetes: 2023 Update (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Life-sustaining therapy (Canada Revenue Agency); Disability-Related Information 2025 (RC4064) (Canada Revenue Agency); Registered Disability Savings Plan: how to apply (Employment and Social Development Canada); Insulin Pump Access Program (Québec) (Gouvernement du Québec); Insulin Pump Program (Saskatchewan) (Government of Saskatchewan); Chronic Kidney Disease in Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Type 1 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines)

### 03 · Your child at school
Group: **Seasons of life** · Referral chip: **Ask your child’s school** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `schoolLowKit` — Dex4 Fast Acting Glucose Tablets Tropical Fruit (7371), Dex4 Glucose Gel Fruit Punch (7382), Dex4 Key Chain (4731), 2BEID Medical Alert Bracelets Small (4289)

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- Diabetes Canada says a student’s care plan has two parts: a daily diabetes management plan and a diabetes emergency plan `3.1`
- Diabetes Canada says the principal should work with you, your child and your child’s health care team to write the plan `3.2`
- The Canadian Paediatric Society recommends talking it through before the school year starts, and having at least two staff trained `3.3`
- Diabetes Canada says students should be able to check their blood sugar, take insulin, and treat lows and highs wherever and whenever they need to `3.4`
- Diabetes Canada says schools should let students carry a phone or smartwatch to help manage their blood sugar `3.5`
- Diabetes@School says lows at school are common for students with type 1. They’re no cause for alarm, but they need treating right away, where they happen `3.6`
- Don’t leave a student alone if a low is suspected. If they’re unresponsive, have a seizure or can’t take sugar by mouth, it’s an emergency: have someone call 911, turn them on their side, stay with them, and put nothing in their mouth `3.7`
- Then, if the care plan includes consent for glucagon, staff named in the plan, and trained, give it `3.8`
- Diabetes Canada’s 2025 type 1 guideline calls for help with giving insulin at school and daycare across Canada `3.9`

> **Note** `3.note` — School rules differ by province and territory, and Diabetes Canada compares them. Diabetes@School, from the Canadian Paediatric Society and its partners, has more for families and school staff.

*Sources for this card:* Kids with Diabetes in School (Diabetes Canada); Managing type 1 diabetes in school (CPS position statement, 2015) (Canadian Paediatric Society); Low blood sugar: What it is, and what to do (Diabetes@School (Canadian Paediatric Society, CPEG and Diabetes Canada)); Glucagon: What it is and how to use it (Diabetes@School (Canadian Paediatric Society, CPEG and Diabetes Canada)); Glycemic Management Across the Lifespan for People With Type 1 Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Comparisons by Province/Territory (Diabetes Canada)

### 04 · Later life
Group: **Seasons of life** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `laterLife` — Accu-Chek Guide Meter (4556), Contour NEXT ONE Meter (4524), Nano PRO Pen Needles 4mm 32G (4777)

- Diabetes Canada’s guideline for older people sets targets by how healthy and independent someone is `4.1`
- For people who are healthy and independent, the A1C target is 7.0% or lower `4.2`
- For people who take medicine that can cause lows, the guideline says a less strict A1C target may be considered: 7.1 to 8.0% for people who are functionally dependent, and 7.1 to 8.5% for people who are frail or living with dementia. Your team sets yours. Near the end of life, the guideline says A1C tests are no longer recommended. The aim then is to avoid any lows, and highs that cause symptoms `4.3`
- The guideline puts a strong focus on preventing lows in older people `4.4`
- If injecting is getting harder, ask your team about simpler options. The guideline names prefilled insulin pens as one way to cut down on dose mistakes `4.5`
- Changes in memory or thinking can make a new skill, like injecting, harder to learn. Tell your team, so they can plan around it `4.6`
- In Ontario, people 65 and older who use insulin every day and live at home can apply to the Assistive Devices Program for $170 a year toward syringes and needles `4.7`

> **Note** `4.note` — Ask a pharmacist to go through your full list of medicines, including anything you buy without a prescription. More programs for seniors are in Funding & Coverage. This card draws on Diabetes Canada’s guideline for health professionals and its key messages for older people.

*Sources for this card:* Diabetes in Older People (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Targets for Glycemic Control (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Diabetes equipment and supplies (Government of Ontario)

### 05 · Caring for someone with diabetes
Group: **Care and community** · Referral chip: **Ask someone who’s been there ✎** · Products shown: *none*

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- The most useful things to learn are what a low and a high look like, the Rule of 15, and when to call for help. They’re all in Staying Safe `5.1`
- If they have glucagon, ask to be shown how it works. Diabetes Canada’s guideline says the people around them should be taught `5.2`
- Ask what kind of help is wanted before you offer it `5.3`
- Breakthrough T1D has a caregiver guide for parents and caregivers of children and teens with type 1 `5.4`
- Its Mental Health + Diabetes Directory lists registered mental health providers, for people living with diabetes and the people affected by it `5.5`
- Low mood and worry about lows are common with diabetes, and Diabetes Canada’s guideline asks teams to check for them `5.6`

> **Note** `5.note` — If caring is wearing you down, tell your own doctor. Diabetes Canada’s guideline says parents and caregivers of young people with diabetes should be checked for diabetes distress too. *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

*Sources for this card:* Chapter 14: 2023 Update – Hypoglycemia in Adults (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Mental Health Support (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Taking care of your mental health (Diabetes Canada); Mental Health and Diabetes: 2023 Update (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); 9-8-8: Suicide Crisis Helpline (9-8-8: Suicide Crisis Helpline (Canada))

### 06 · First Nations and Inuit: NIHB coverage
Group: **Care and community** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist** · Products shown: *none*

- Indigenous Services Canada runs the federal Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program for First Nations and Inuit `6.1`
- Who is eligible is set out on Indigenous Services Canada’s eligibility page. Liivv can’t decide whether you’re eligible. For questions about eligibility, Indigenous Services Canada says to contact your NIHB regional office `6.2`
- For people who manage diabetes with insulin, NIHB covers several continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), with prior approval. The list is in the NIHB program updates `6.3`
- It also covers up to 800 test strips every 100 days for people who use insulin `6.4`
- If you aren’t covered by NIHB, Funding & Coverage lists the programs in each province and territory `6.5`

> **Note** `6.note` — NIHB adds items to its list from time to time. Your pharmacist can check what’s covered today.

*Sources for this card:* Who is eligible for the Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program for First Nations and Inuit (Indigenous Services Canada (Non-Insured Health Benefits)); Non-Insured Health Benefits program updates (Indigenous Services Canada (Non-Insured Health Benefits))

- **eyebrow** `pharmacist.eyebrow` — Anywhere in Canada
- **heading** `pharmacist.heading` — Supply questions, whoever you’re shopping for
- **body** `pharmacist.body` — The Certified Diabetes Educators at Bayshore Express Pharmacy, the Liivv pharmacy in Markham, Ontario, answer questions from anywhere in Canada: pumps, sensors, meters, supplies, billing and claims. When needed, they pass you to the Liivv pharmacy in your province. Questions about a pregnancy, a child’s plan or a change in someone’s health belong with their diabetes team.

## Closing

**The same diabetes, a different season** `closing.heading`

What changes is who to bring in, and when. Knowing that is most of the work. `closing.body`

## Disclaimer

This is general information, not medical advice. Care in pregnancy, for children and in later life differs in ways this page doesn’t try to cover. It tells you what changes and who to ask. Your diabetes team sets your targets and your plan. `disclaimer`

Reviewer-only: none of this renders on a page.*
